name: Silesian

ancestors.notes: Descent from Proto-Slavic (West Slavic, Lechitic / Silesian subgroup).
Closely related Lechitic neighbour; language-vs-dialect classification disputed.
German adstrate: Silesia long under Bohemian/Prussian rule; very heavy lexical layer.
Czech adstrate along the Moravian-Silesian border.

notes: Silesian (Ślůnski), West Slavic variety spoken in Silesia (Poland/Czech Republic). Classification as language vs. Polish dialect debated. Distinctive vowels ô /o/ and the palatal sibilants ś, ź. German loanword influence significant. No single standard orthography.

sources.author: Jaroszewicz, Henryk
sources.title: Standardization of the Silesian Language: The Current Status and Prospects for Development
sources.publisher: Poznańskie Studia Polonistyczne. Seria Językoznawcza 30(1), 57-72 (open access)
sources.notes: Read in full. p. 61 describes the orthography adopted in Cieszyn in 2009 and elaborated in the 2010 Gōrnoślōnski ślabikŏrz: Polish-style ⟨ch h ó u rz ż dź ł⟩ and ⟨ś si ć ci ź zi dź dzi⟩ for the soft series, plus ⟨ō⟩ for the closed [ȯ] absent from Polish and the two homographs ⟨ŏ⟩ and ⟨ô⟩ that unify dialectally different realisations. p. 65 tabulates the model versus optional spellings of the 2022-2023 Principles of Silesian Language Spelling (o:ŏ, o:õ, a:ã, ym:am, and the rest). This source contradicts two things this spec says: its notes call the orthography unstandardised, while a standard has existed since 2009 with a revision under way, and the map's single ⟨ô⟩ = /o/ leaves ⟨ō⟩, ⟨ŏ⟩, ⟨õ⟩ and ⟨ã⟩ unread. Recorded here; the grapheme data is not changed in this citation.

stress.notes: Silesian (szl) follows the Polish penultimate stress pattern. Diacritics ô ō ŏ mark vowel quality, not stress. Source: Pattern consistent with Polish (pl); note that Silesian is a dialect continuum and individual varieties may vary. Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silesian_language
